pattern: flood before the (seller|owner) (bought|owned)[^.]{0,40}(is not|isn't|never) asked|form (never|does not|doesn't) ask[^.]{0,60}(earlier|past|prior|older) flood
struck: A flood before the seller bought is not asked.
use: Four of the form's flood questions ask only about the seller's own years of ownership. No question asks directly about a flood before the seller bought, though question 23 asks about any flood risk the seller knows of.

pattern: (bank|lender) selling a (home|house) it took back|(home|house) (a|the) (bank|lender) took back
struck: Many sales need no form at all: an estate or trust sale, a foreclosure, a bank selling a home it took back, a public auction.
use: Some sales need no form at all: an estate or trust sale, a foreclosure, a lender selling a home it bought at a foreclosure sale, a public auction.

unless: prevailing|whichever side wins|side that wins|winning side
struck: A court may also award attorney fees.
use: The court may also award reasonable attorney fees to whichever side wins.

struck: A clean report can also mean an insurer did not report.
use: (cut it: no source)

struck: The CLUE report covers up to seven years.
use: Only the owner, an insurer or a lender can order the claims report (CLUE). It covers only recent years.

struck: A severe repetitive loss house has four or more paid claims over $5,000 each, or two or more building payments that add up to more than the house is worth, counted since 1978.
use: A severe repetitive loss house has four or more paid claims over $5,000 each, or two or more building payments that add up to more than the house is worth, with at least two of them within 10 years of each other, counted since 1978.

struck: A house FEMA calls a severe repetitive loss pays a 15 percent surcharge.
use: A house FEMA calls a severe repetitive loss pays a 15 percent surcharge, or the prior-claims charge if that is higher.

struck: In the Socastee area, the state's voluntary buyout program set out to buy 61 flood-damaged homes, has closed on 52, and tears the houses down.
use: The state's voluntary buyout program began in Socastee with a goal of 61 homes that flooded again and again. By mid-2024 it had bought 52 homes in Horry County, and it tears the houses down so the land goes back to open green space.

struck: FEMA grants have paid for flooded homes to be bought and cleared here before: 63 buildings after Hurricane Floyd.
use: FEMA grant projects here have listed flood-prone buildings to buy: 63 after Hurricane Floyd and 86 in Conway after Hurricane Matthew. A Florence project, approved but not finished, lists 8 more.

struck: The Florence flood map covers 157.5 square miles of the county.
use: The Florence flood map covers about 157 square miles of the county.

struck: About 1 in 4 (2,047, or 23 percent) were on buildings rated outside the high-risk flood zone.
use: Nearly 1 in 4 (2,047, or 23 percent) were on buildings rated outside the high-risk flood zone.

struck: On FEMA's current map, half of those buildings (433 of 863) are still outside it.
use: On FEMA's current map, half of Florence's paid claims (433 of 863) are on buildings outside the high-risk zone. Of the 391 rated outside, 376 are outside it on today's map too.

struck: Polo Farms near Longs had five feet of water in homes.
use: Polo Farms, off SC 905, had five feet of water in homes; Aberdeen Country Club in Longs and Bradford Creek off SC 544 had up to three feet.

struck: Only about 1 in 7 homes in Horry County has a federal flood policy.
use: FEMA's take-up rate for flood insurance on homes in Horry County is about 15 percent, about one policy for every seven residential buildings.

struck: In Horry County's high-risk zone that means raising the lowest floor at least three feet above the base flood height.
use: In an AE zone in unincorporated Horry County, that means the lowest floor at least three feet above the base flood height.

pattern: paid on (it )?more than once|(about|more than|over) (1|one) in (5|five)[^.]{0,30}203
struck: FEMA lists 1,094 properties in Horry County that flood insurance has paid on more than once. About 1 in 5 (203) are outside the high-risk zone.
use: FEMA lists 1,094 properties in Horry County on its repeat-loss list. Nearly 1 in 5 (203) are outside the high-risk zone.

pattern: (?<!about )three years after Florence|(Horry County|the county) and (all )?its towns
struck: FEMA's current flood maps for Horry County and its towns took effect three years after Florence.
use: FEMA's current flood maps for Horry County and the towns with a mapped high-risk zone took effect about three years after Florence.

struck: A seller's federal flood policy can usually move to the buyer at the sale, which can keep its rate.
use: In some cases a seller's federal flood policy can be transferred to the buyer at the sale.

pattern: next round of (federal )?aid|(does not|doesn't|fails to) (tell|notify)[^.]{0,40}can owe
struck: A seller who does not tell can owe the government the next round of aid.
use: If the seller does not, and the buyer then goes without flood insurance and later receives federal disaster aid for flood damage, the seller must repay that aid.

struck: About 36 to 59 manufactured homes sit there, and about 2,100 houses sit inside the county's Florence flood map.
use: More than 2,000 houses sit inside the county's Florence flood map.

struck: For those houses, the seller's form never asks about Florence.
use: For those houses, the form's flood-history questions cover only years after Florence.

pattern: three years[^.]{0,80}(knew or should have known)
struck: South Carolina sets deadlines for lawsuits, often three years, counted from when you knew or should have known.
use: South Carolina sets deadlines for these claims; many are three years, and for fraud the time starts when the fraud is discovered. Ask an attorney now.

pattern: rain and river floods do not
struck: Storm surge floods mostly stay inside FEMA's high-risk zone here; rain and river floods do not.
use: Storm surge claims here stay almost all inside FEMA's high-risk zone. Rain and river floods reach outside it far more often: 37 to 51 percent of paid claims.
